I have received the exposition of the *Vajracchedikā* you sent. Upon reading it, I cannot help but admire how you, Elder Brother, have synthesized the various commentaries on this scripture throughout both ancient and modern times. ... [The text continues with the author's reflections on the nature of the commentary and its relationship to the original sūtra] ... Incense is formed into pellets; by weaving together many strands of silk, one creates brocade. Delight in taking up the virtues of others, and do not rely upon your own excellence.
With a mind fixed upon the Mahāyāna and the Supreme Vehicle, you are like an *udumbara* flower of the present age; there are truly great people within the Confucian school.

Commentaries on the sutras are difficult to compose, and this sutra is particularly difficult to comment upon. If one were to explain this sutra for others like a timely teacher, it would not even be considered [an ordinary act].

It is difficult to comment upon this sutra; yet, one should aspire to master it thoroughly and penetrate its depths so as not to lose the Buddha’s intent, lest one fall into the grave error of slandering the Buddha—this is the most difficult of difficulties.
It would be better to contemplate only the general meaning than to follow one's own unguided intellect; it would be better to leave matters in doubt than to provide groundless annotations.

The entire sutra consists of only five thousand one hundred and forty-six characters. Prince Zhaoming divided it into thirty-two sections, while Bodhiruci divided it... [text ends] ...into [sections].

The twelve sections, Vasubandhu’s eighteen abodes, Asaṅga’s twenty-seven doubts, and Maitreya’s eighty verses—these were composed by the Bodhisattva Guṇaprabha as a treatise, with the Venerable Master Fu composing the verses and others;
when they were examined by Fuyan through the Buddha-eye of transcendence.
It is as vast as the entirety of the realm of empty space. Tradition holds that during the early Tang dynasty, there were as many as eight hundred commentaries on this sutra;

because so much time has passed, they can no longer be seen. Prior to these were the commentary by Zhiyi of Tiantai, and following them were the compendium by Guifeng, the collected explanations by Yang Gui, the annotated record by Changshui, the abridged meanings by Zhongfeng, and those by Zongle.

Regarding these commentaries and the sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) of the present day, they already fill entire bookshelves. As for the "dark pearl of the dark waters," who can truly determine what it represents?
To trace its origins, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was taught following the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* scriptures; it consists of six hundred fascicles across sixteen assemblies in four locations.
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* is one of these, spoken during the ninth assembly. Regarding this *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*:
Upon entering China, there were a total of six translations made over time, one of which was that of the Qin dynasty.
The Sūtra possesses a great head and major limbs, with blood and marrow filling it completely and perfectly within. What is meant by the "great head"?
It is what the Sūtra calls the Vajra; none other than this, it is the *tathatā*-mind of both sentient beings and Buddhas. This *tathatā*-mind is unchanging.

It accords with conditions; yet, while it accords with conditions, it does not change. That which does not change is this True Suchness-mind (tathatā-citta), common to both sentient beings and Buddhas.
Swords cannot cut it; fire cannot burn it. It can destroy all things, yet nothing can destroy it. Therefore, there are a hundred parables regarding Prajñāpāramitā.
This single metaphor is like a vajra; it may also be given the provisional name "unconditioned dharmas following conditions.
All things—saints and ordinary beings alike, as well as their environments and bodies—exist through unconditioned dharmas, yet they exhibit distinctions and are thus termed "conditioned dharmas.

These are likened to dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning; they should not be grasped or attached to, for they belong to the gate of arising and ceasing. Regarding this sutra, I have long...
A bitter thicket of complications; until now, I have grown old amidst anxieties and tribulations. Reading it, I have gained a slight glimpse of its essence.
Rather than speaking deeply, it is better to speak superficially; rather than speaking in abstruse and remote terms, it is better to speak with plain and practical clarity.
Every sentence of the entire scripture is earnest and flowing, layered upon layer, like the interconnected bones of a skeleton or the encircling embrace of a coiled serpent.
Sand. After all, where is the head? Does not the Buddha say in the sutra, "All dharmas are without self"?
I venture to say that of these five thousand one hundred and forty-six characters in the scripture, I have only been able to comment upon these five words.

Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. When True Suchness does not maintain itself, movement gives rise to ignorance; it is simply this "self" that constitutes the great affliction.
The mark of self; the view of self; "I am able to deliver sentient beings"; "I am able to practice giving"; "I am able to attain the fruit";
"I am able to preach the Dharma"; "I am able to bestow predictions of enlightenment"; "I am able to adorn Buddha-lands";
"I am able to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges"; "I am able to sacrifice my body and life"; "I am able to uphold the precepts. I am able...
"I am patient. "I am able to practice wholesome dharmas. "I am able to accumulate merit and virtue. These points I have not forgotten.

From this arises the attachment to a self, the attachment to dharmas as real, and the attachment to dharmas as non-real; the attachment to the primary retribution, and the attachment to the secondary environment;

the boasting of one's achievements and competing for ability; the disparaging of others' goodness and the flaunting of one's own toil; and the longing for blessings and profit, thereby acting as a superior.
It is because they fall into attachment to giving; it is because they are held in contempt by others; it is because their contention is stubborn. This is what is called a "unified characteristic.
This is what is called "all minds are not mind. This is what is called "abiding in non-abiding," yet not abiding in *prajñā*.
This is what is called "being subdued by afflictions," yet being unable to subdue the afflictions.
I am like a fortified city, and [the afflictions] are like enemies who surround me for thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas with a firm and impenetrable siege.

It is as if a person has entered the darkness and sees nothing at all. Truly, there are those capable of giving rise to the bodhicitta and generating a pure mind that does not dwell in the six sense-objects;

they generate a mind that should have no place of abiding, and they generate a mind toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Whenever they deliver sentient beings or practice generosity, they obtain the fruit thereof.

Preaching the Dharma and adorning the lands; upholding the precepts, practicing patience, and accumulating merit and so forth. With penetrating wisdom-illumination, he contemplates deliverance yet there is nothing delivered;
he contemplates giving yet there is nothing given; he contemplates attainment yet there is nothing attained; he contemplates preaching yet there is nothing preached;

he contemplates recording [the teachings] yet there is nothing recorded; he contemplates adornment yet there is nothing adorned; he contemplates making offerings yet there is nothing offered; he contemplates his own body and life.
Yet there is no body or life. One contemplates the observance of precepts and finds no observance of precepts; one contemplates patience and finds no patience;
one contemplates wholesome dharmas and finds no wholesome dharmas; one contemplates merit and finds no merit; one contemplates atoms and finds no atoms;
one contemplates worlds and finds no worlds; one contemplates the four marks and finds no four marks; one contemplates the four views and finds no four views. This is the ultimate sanctity.
All phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants are ultimately subsumed within the single True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, conditioned dharmas are realized as unconditioned dharmas;

and by means of the provisional self, one perceives the true, eternal self. Dwelling as a traveler in this world, one should be without intentional grasping and must certainly be free from a fixed self. As for those who boast of their achievements among the common folk—

How could one contend with or greedily cling to it? When its habitual perfumation is thoroughly exhausted to its very source and bottom, there is a sudden, vast clearing away—like the light of the sun illuminating all manner of forms.
At that moment, the solid fortress is pulverized and the enemy’s weapons are turned back. Mind after mind is *prajñā*;
everywhere is the *vajra*. This is the ultimate person who has no self, the spiritual person who has no merit, and the sage who has no name.
Therefore it is said: "A Bodhisattva who penetrates the dharma of non-self—the Tathāgata calls such a one a true Bodhisattva.
Regarding this, which constitutes the primary heading of the entire sutra, I dare not say that I have pierced its very red heart; yet perhaps, though I have not hit the mark, I am not far from it.
What are the great structural divisions? First, following the sections of the sūtra to avoid censure; second, indicating the purport of the sūtra to highlight its essentials;
third, summarizing the imagery of the sūtra to accord with the text; fourth, synthesizing the intent of the sūtra to grasp its direction;

and fifth, opening the eye of the sūtra to dispel doubts. What is meant by "following the sections of the sūtra"? It means that throughout the entire sūtra, the question resides within the answer, and the answer resides within the question.
It is as if a divine dragon appears and disappears, its limits impossible to discern. However, regarding the hand that dots the eyes, one merely sketches the body and head of the dragon;

those parts that wind and coil amidst the mist and clouds need not all be drawn in full detail. Herein, following the divisions of the text, I have minutely examined the "coming dragon" (the source of the lineage):
from the second section, where Subhūti rises from among the great assembly, up to the fourth section, where it says, "A bodhisattva should simply be like... [and so forth].
Regarding the place where the teaching is established: it takes the "Dragon's Head" chapter as its entirety.

For the meaning of dwelling in the mind and subduing [the passions] constitutes the primary doctrine, just as the "Great Learning" and the "Chapter on the Mandate of Heaven" in the *Zhongyong* encompass the essential purport of their respective scriptures.
From the fifth section, "One may see the Tathāgata through the marks of the body without arising," up to the sixteenth section, "Retribution is also not... [the text continues].

This concludes the section on "The Thinkable" (*cintya*). It is like the division of chapters in the *Xue* and *Yong* sections of the *Zhongyong*, which repeatedly clarifies the meaning of stabilizing the mind and subduing it.
From the seventeenth section onward, Subhūti raises the principle of stabilizing the mind and subduing it as the opening inquiry.

Various schools have offered diverse and convoluted interpretations with empty minds; yet upon careful investigation, none are definitive. This is precisely like the [commentary on] the *Nanhua jing* (Zhuangzi) by Bei...
The "One Fish in the Abyss" appears twice within the "On Carefree Wandering"; though the words are repeated, the essential flavor remains no different.
Following these seventeen sections, it is repeatedly stated that there is no dharma to be attained, and it is repeatedly stated that the great body is no body at all.
The nineteenth chapter reiterates the discussion on adornment and non-adornment. The twentieth chapter reiterates the merit of giving.
The twenty-first chapter reiterates that the Tathāgata has no dharma to preach.
The twenty-fourth chapter reiterates the merit of preaching this sutra. The twenty-fifth chapter...
It is said that, in reality, there are no sentient beings to be liberated. In the twenty-sixth section, it is reiterated that the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks.
In the thirtieth section, it is reiterated that [the Buddha] is neither atoms nor worlds.

As for other passages where it is not reiterated, the words and phrases therein are likewise multiple; this is because Indian speech and sounds are inherently repetitive, and because the Buddha’s compassion is profound and deep. It is not...
This contradicts their local customs; therefore, there are no such expressions as "without marks," "without views," "without teaching," "without attainment," "without deliverance," or "without merit.

These terms appear sometimes three or five times, or eight or nine times; they are spoken repeatedly either for the sake of instructing those of dull faculties or for reiterating them for those who arrive later.
One never tires of repeating them, nor is there any actual divergence added to them. This may be due to errors in translation or corruptions in the transcription, but it is merely that.

One should firmly maintain faith and seek the Buddha’s empowerment; then, naturally, there will come the moment when one is like the cook Dingfeng, who carves through oxen, peeling away the great and opening the great cavities.
If, as various schools insist, one must dispute over discrepancies between earlier and later passages, then let them be resolved accordingly.
Even where there is no point of difficulty, one insists on resolving it; by forcing the text, one gives rise to arbitrary and far-fetched interpretations.

With such a mass of doubts piled up, even the Buddha’s own words might as well be hung on the wall. If one truly knows how to interpret them, would one encounter such a person only once every morning or evening?

Unless one’s understanding does not err from the Buddha’s intent, the karmic retribution for slander is grave; how could one ever achieve purification through repentance? This scripture must be followed according to its divisions. [This marks the end of the scripture.]

What is the essential meaning? Every sutra that is initiated must have a fundamental principle. In this sutra, the Buddha, during the assembly at Vulture Peak, refuted conventional discourse by means of emptiness;
through supreme, perfect, and complete enlightenment, he expounded the emptiness of persons, the emptiness of phenomena, and the emptiness of both phenomena and non-phenomena.
Ordinary people cannot sever delusions, and those of the Two Vehicles cannot transform consciousness. There are two reasons for this: first, they abide in the attainment of realization;

second, they abide in merit alone. When the First Patriarch came from the West, he swept away the attachment to realization, saying, "Vast emptiness—there is no sage," and he swept away the attachment to merit, saying, "There is no merit whatsoever.
I venture to say that the purport of the Buddha’s teaching in this sutra is likewise concise and essential.
However, upon examining the scriptural texts as a whole, it is as if there is neither attainment nor teaching. I did not harbor the thought, "I am an Arhat.
At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I truly attained nothing regarding the Dharma. Regarding *samyaksaṃbodhi*, there is not the slightest dharma that can be attained.
Truly, there is no dharma by which one gives rise to the bodhicitta. To see forms or seek through sounds is...
This is a deviant path. Is this not what is meant by "vast emptiness, wherein there is no sage"? Merit and virtue equal to empty space cannot be measured or conceived.
The gift of the seven treasures throughout the three-thousandfold world system does not approach it; the gift of one’s own body and life does not approach it;
and the gift of one’s body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, offered at the three times of day, does not approach the merit of making offerings to nayutas of Buddhas.
They do not equal it. This merit is not the nature of merit. The various Bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Is this not what is meant by "having no meritorious virtue"? The Buddha takes pity on those of the Hīnayāna, who are deluded by the mind that seeks something to attain.
Deluded and ignorant ordinary beings are misled by the causes of tainted outflows that lead to the minor fruits of human and celestial rebirth.

They fall into the dual obstacles of afflictions and the known, which consist of the perception of a self and the clinging to a self; they fall into the two types of death—segmented and transformative—within and beyond the realms.

From birth to birth, they fail to attain purity. One must not shrink from employing manifold methods of refinement, just as one must first wash a vessel clean before it can hold celestial nectar. Zhao.

What the Prefect said—“I do not like to hear the word ‘Buddha’”—and what Pang Yun meant by “For hundreds of thousands of lifetimes I have been burdened by my practice of giving,” both capture the essential purport of this sutra.

Regarding the structure of the sutra, it must be divided into three sections: there is the introduction (nidāna), the main body (samyak-saṃbuddha-kāya), and finally the conclusion and circulation (pariṇāmanā). This sutra...
The Thirteenth Division. Śūnyatā-utpanna requests the Buddha to bestow titles and conclude the sutra.

This section, which praises the half-worldly and extols the supreme state of the Dharma, constitutes the dissemination (*pravartana*) and does not belong to the end of the sutra; only as such does it serve as the dissemination.

According to the division of the text into "elephant" units, each section explains one cycle of the sutra, interspersed with one cycle of comparing merits. In total, there are seven layers of merit. The first layer:
The merit of non-abiding is the merit of seeing one's nature. The subsequent five layers of merit each increase in excellence;
each layer constitutes, in general, merit with signs (*sanimitta-puṇya*). Compared to the merit of seeing one's nature, these truly cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.

The final four sections represent the Buddha’s accommodation to the capacities of sentient beings, wherein he refutes and dispels the ordinary person's attachments to the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*). At the end, [he addresses] all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
A single verse of the Dharma encompasses the entire sutra; therefore, it is not divided into a "Correct Teaching" (śarīra) nor a "Circulation" (parivarta).

The protective mindfulness and entrustment are as poignant as a mother’s heart. It is like a formal school with its ranks in perfect order; it is like a garland of flowers, like scattered blossoms, like right wisdom, and like skillful means.
It is like reaching the end of mountains and the exhaustion of waters—sitting and watching the clouds rise. This is the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra.
Regarding this essential summary: what is the convergence of the sutra’s meaning? Generally, when the Buddha preached a sutra, one understands its intent by following its words and phrases.
This sutra is titled *Vajra* (The Diamond), yet the text speaks of "non-contention," "patience," "freedom from anger and resentment," "accepting contempt," and "attaining the perfection of patience.
Thus, it does not take "hardness" as being hard; it is purely through gentleness.
This is for the sake of firmness; this is the Buddha’s intention. The Buddha said: "The Tathāgata has no dharma that he teaches.
The Tathāgata has no fixed dharma to teach. The Tathāgata has no dharma that can be taught. If one says that the Tathāgata has a dharma that he teaches, that is to slander the Buddha."
Furthermore, the sutra emphasizes faith, understanding, and upholding; it emphasizes copying, reciting, and reading; and it emphasizes upholding even as few as four lines of verse.
It states "explaining for others" four times, "expounding for others" twice, "extensively expounding for others" once, and "proclaiming for others" once.
It further states: "The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out in the Mahāyāna."
This was spoken by one who has set forth upon the Supreme Vehicle. It is further said: "The Tathāgata speaks words that are true, real, as-it-is, non-deceptive, and non-contradictory.
How could he speak when silent, or remain silent when speaking? Would the Tathāgata have his own words contradict themselves?

As for the statement "there is no dharma to be spoken," this is intended specifically for those who are attached to words; it means that one does not abandon words while seeking to explain liberation. Although...
Furthermore, it does not rely on the path of language, nor does it cling to the absence of speech; this is the intention of the Buddha. The Sūtra states:
"Whatever has characteristics is all false and illusory. It says that if one sees that all characteristics are non-characteristics, one sees the Tathāgata.
It says that being free from all characteristics is what is called the Buddhas. And yet it also says: "All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Furthermore—
It says: "The teachings of all Buddhas emerge from this sutra. It also says: "Cultivate all wholesome dharmas by means of non-self, non-person, non-sentient-being, and non-life-span.

It further says: "One who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the mark of annihilation regarding dharmas. And it says: "To achieve that which is most supreme, foremost, and rare..."
The Dharma. It is further said: "One accomplishes the most rare and extraordinary merit. It is also said: "One accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit.
It is also said: "One accomplishes merit that is unfathomable, incomparable, limitless, and inconceivable."
It is further said: "The Buddha-dharma is neither real nor unreal; it establishes while sweeping away, and sweeps away while establishing. Does the Tathāgata have the faults of the world? No.
This is to exhaustively eliminate the unreality of views and appearances, thereby clearly manifesting the reality of Prajñā. This is the intention of the Buddha."
The Sūtra says: "I shall bring all sentient beings to extinction through *nirvāṇa* without remainder. However, the sentient beings of the ten realms are but the mind alone;
they are illusory and false, like the phantom figures produced by pressing on the eyes.

When people perceive these appearances and cannot purify them, thoughts arise, and thus immeasurable sentient beings are born. Since one is not separate from these sentient beings, how can one deliver them?
Therefore, in another sutra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Within a single day and night in your minds, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings arise and perish.
If you can use wisdom to illuminate them so that thoughts do not arise in succession, this is precisely to have delivered all sentient beings."

Thus one knows that sentient beings have both the provisional degree (sāṃvṛtika-yāna) and the ultimate degree (pāramārthika-yāna). There are those who deliver sentient beings of the world, and there are those who deliver their own minds.
There are those who deliver by gathering them in accordance with [their nature], and there are those who deliver by subduing them through opposition.

All these arise from the ultimate reality (li-jù) before they manifest as provisional function (shi-yòng). They necessarily require the internal and external illumination of wisdom; only when one has "exhausted the person and exhausted things," as in Confucianism, does one truly achieve this.

Nirvana without remainder is not like that of the followers of the Lesser Vehicle who delight in inferior teachings. Therefore it is said: "All sentient beings are, in truth, no sentient beings. It is said:
"They are neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings. It is said: "The Tathāgata says they are no sentient beings; they are called 'sentient beings' by name. It is said:
"In reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers. Such is the intention of the Buddha. All such statements as these are...
